# A lakehouse table inside Postgres

Analytical queries, the kind that scan millions of rows to sum a few columns, run slowly on the
row tables an application uses. The previous chapter answered that by copying rows out of Postgres
into a columnar database. [pg_ducklake](https://github.com/relytcloud/pg_ducklake) takes the
opposite route and brings the columnar table into Postgres. One statement makes a columnar copy of a
table:

```sql
CREATE TABLE events_lake USING ducklake AS SELECT * FROM events;
```

The new table uses the [DuckLake](https://ducklake.select) format, which splits a table in two. The
rows are written as Parquet files, a columnar file format. The catalog, which records the files
that make up the table, their statistics and every snapshot, is ordinary tables in the `ducklake`
schema of the same database. Queries that touch the table run in DuckDB, an analytical engine that
the extension runs inside the Postgres backend.

One database can then hold row tables for the application and column tables for analytics, and a
single query can join them. The lab runs it as the `ducklake` server on port 5443, from the
upstream image `pgducklake/pgducklake:18-v1.0.2` (Postgres 18.4, extension preloaded). The notebook
measures it on five million events.

## The trade, measured

The notebook builds the same table twice. `events_heap` is an ordinary Postgres table (a heap)
with a primary key, and `events_lake` is a copy made with `USING ducklake`.

| | heap | DuckLake |
|---|---|---|
| on disk | 301 MB, plus a 107 MB primary key | 78 MB, one Parquet file |
| sum of amount by device | 159 ms | 33 ms |
| daily distinct users | 1,618 ms | 774 ms |
| top ten users by spend | 453 ms | 52 ms |
| one row by id | 0.12 ms | 13 ms |

The three analytical queries read a few columns of every row, which is what Parquet is laid out
for. DuckDB reads only those columns, compressed, in vectors of 2,048 values. It comes out 2 to 9
times faster than the heap, even though Postgres runs the heap scans with two parallel workers.

The last row is the other side of the trade. A lake table has no index. To fetch one row, DuckDB
skips the files and row groups whose min/max statistics rule it out, then scans what is left. The
heap only has to descend a B-tree. Keep the rows the application reads one at a time in heap
tables.

## Writes on immutable files

Parquet files are never changed in place, so small writes would leave many tiny files. DuckLake
avoids that in two ways.

An insert below a row limit is **inlined**. Its rows go into a Postgres table in the catalog, and
queries read them alongside the Parquet. A flush, or the extension's background worker, writes them
out to Parquet later.

An update or delete writes a **delete file**, which names the row positions that no longer count.
In the notebook, updating 1,000 rows and deleting 1,663 left the 78 MB data file untouched. It
added a 14 kB delete file and a 19 kB file with the updated rows.

## Snapshots, time travel and a change feed

Every commit is a snapshot in the catalog, with a note of what it changed. Any snapshot that has
not been expired can be read back, and two functions do the reading:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM ducklake.time_travel('events_lake'::regclass, 5) t;
SELECT * FROM ducklake.table_changes('events_lake'::regclass, 8, 9);
```

After the update and delete, the table had 4,998,337 rows, and its snapshot from before them still
had 5,000,001. `table_changes` returns the rows inserted, updated and deleted between two
snapshots, which is the input an incremental job downstream needs.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A rough edge in 1.0.2

`table_changes` over a range that contains a delete fails with `function struct_pack(...) does not
exist`. Afterwards, that connection's DuckDB has lost its catalog until it reconnects, and even
`DROP TABLE` fails. Ranges of inserts work, so the notebook stays on those.
:::

## Partitions, and when they help

`CALL ducklake.set_partition('events_part'::regclass, 'device')` makes later writes split their
files by device, so that a filter on device can skip whole files. On a local disk at this size it
bought nothing, with 28 ms for the partitioned table against 30 ms for the single file. Reading one
compressed column of a 78 MB file is already cheap, and the row-group statistics inside the file do
part of a partition's job.

Partitions pay off on object storage, where a skipped file is a skipped download.
`ducklake.default_table_path` points the files at S3, GCS, R2 or Azure.

## Joining rows and columns

A lake table joins any Postgres table in plain SQL. DuckDB plans the whole statement and reads the
heap side through its own Postgres scan. A condensed version of the plan shows both scans:

```text
HASH_JOIN  user_id = user_id
├── DUCKLAKE_SCAN            Table: events_lake   Projections: user_id
└── PGDUCKDB_POSTGRES_SCAN   Table: users         Projections: user_id, pro
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## DuckLake or Doris

pg_ducklake keeps one database and one transaction boundary. The analytical table is written by the
same SQL as everything else and needs no pipeline. Doris is a second system to run, but it scales
out on its own hardware and keeps analytical load off the primary. A Postgres server running DuckDB
queries is still one server, so heavy analytics there compete with the application for CPU and
memory.
:::

The [pg_ducklake playground](../notebooks/pg_ducklake_playground.ipynb) notebook measures every
number in this chapter.
